Chapter 03

The toolchain: sv, the checks, and the agent beside you

The tools around the code. The sv CLI that scaffolds a project and adds integrations to it, and the one line that reproduces this project’s tooling; svelte-check and every flag worth knowing; ESLint and Prettier; and the Svelte AI tools — instructions, an MCP server, skills and a subagent — with a script that runs the autofixer over every component on every build.

By the end of this chapter

Know what sv create, sv add and sv check do and which of their flags matter, read the lint, format and check configuration and say why each piece is there, and set up an editor or an agent so that what it writes is checked the way this project checks its own code.

The previous chapter walked the workspace; this one walks the tools that work *on* it. None of them is in the app a traveller downloads. All of them decide what reaches it: the CLI that would have written the first version of half these files, the checker that refuses a warning, the linter and formatter that keep every file in one style, and the AI tools that let an agent write Svelte 5 the way this course does rather than the way the internet did in 2022.

sv, the command line

sv is Svelte’s CLI: it creates projects, adds integrations to them, runs migrations and checks the code. The documentation’s advice is to run it through your package manager’s runner — npx sv <command>, or pnpm dlx sv <command> for pnpm — and it says what that does: “If you’re inside a project where sv is already installed, this will use the local installation, otherwise it will download the latest version and run it without installing it.” The download is what you want for sv create, before there is a project to install into. Inside a project, the local installation is what you want, which is why sv is one of this project’s devDependencies, beside @sveltejs/mcp (the AI tools, later in this chapter). Everybody who clones it runs the same version, pnpm exec sv runs it without downloading anything, and an upgrade is a line in package.json that a reviewer can see.

When npx sv seems to do nothing, the CLI’s FAQ names the usual causes: some package managers prefer a locally installed tool to the registry, the name sv collides with runit’s sv on some Linux systems, and Windows PowerShell has a built-in alias sv for Set-Variable. pnpm exec sv in a project that has it installed sidesteps all three.

sv create

sv create [options] [path] scaffolds a SvelteKit project. Run it bare and it asks its questions one at a time; every question also has a flag, so the same project can come from one line in a script or a README. The flags, as sv create --help lists them in 1.1.1:

  • --template <type> — minimal (barebones), demo (a word game that works without JavaScript), library (a package built with svelte-package, the shape packages/waypoint has), or addon (a community add-on for sv itself, ready to test and publish).
  • --types ts, --types jsdoc or --no-types — TypeScript files and lang="ts", JSDoc comments checked by the same compiler, or no type checking at all, which the documentation marks “Not recommended!”.
  • --add <addon...> and --no-add-ons — add-ons to apply as part of the create, in the same syntax as sv add below, or no add-on prompt at all. The help is explicit that the two “cannot be used together”.
  • --install <package-manager> and --no-install — install with npm, yarn, pnpm, bun or deno (1.1.1 also lists pnpm-rush, nub and aube), or do not install.
  • --no-dir-check — scaffold into a folder that is not empty without asking first.
  • --no-download-check — do not warn before downloading a community add-on. Leave it off; the next section says why.
  • --addon-name <name> — the package name for --template addon, as @<org>/<pkg> or <pkg>.
  • --from-playground <url> — create a project from a Svelte playground URL: the CLI downloads its files, detects the dependencies they import, and lays them out as a SvelteKit project.

The line that reproduces this project’s tooling

Meridian was written by hand, file by file, the way the chapters describe. Its *tooling*, though, is exactly what sv would have written, and the two commands below reproduce it — every add-on, with the options this project would have chosen. They were run against sv 1.1.1 while this chapter was written, and the add-on line of the AGENTS.md they produce is the same, character for character, as the one this project carries.

The options use one small syntax, which sv add --help spells out: <addon>=<opt>:<val> sets one option, + joins several (database:sqlite+client:libsql), a comma separates the values of a multi-select (languageTags:en,de,pt-br), and <opt>:none is an explicit empty choice — better-auth="demo:none", because this project writes its own sign-in pages (ch. 34). The help adds the rule that makes a line like this one useful in a script: “To skip prompts, explicitly set ALL options”. And when you do answer the prompts by hand, sv prints the equivalent line at the end, under “To skip prompts next time, run:”, so the interactive run can be written down afterwards.

ai-tools appears twice because it takes one delivery per run. The first run writes the individual tools this project keeps as files — the instructions in AGENTS.md and the MCP configuration — and the second adds the Claude Code plugin, which is what .claude/settings.json enables. The first run deliberately leaves out the svelte-file-editor subagent: the plugin brings its own, and sv itself refuses to let both stand quietly — run the plugin delivery over a project that already has .claude/agents/ and it prints “Claude Code: the Svelte plugin is enabled and .claude/agents also exists - remove it (or disable the plugin) to avoid duplicate skills/sub-agents.” --no-git-check on the second run, because the first has just written every file and nothing is committed yet: the prompt it skips is there to stop you running an add-on over work you have not saved. The record of what was added is the top of AGENTS.md:

Line 6 is the roll-call sv writes, in its order. Lines 3 to 5 were rewritten by hand, because the scaffold can only know “TypeScript” and the package manager, and an agent reading this file should know the versions this project pins and why a peer warning is allowed.

sv add, and what each add-on wrote

sv add applies add-ons to a project that already exists: pnpm exec sv add asks which, pnpm exec sv add prettier eslint does not. Three of its options matter. -C, --cwd <path> points it at another project root — in this workspace, pnpm exec sv add -C packages/waypoint … would apply an add-on to the library rather than the app. --no-git-check skips the prompt about uncommitted changes. --install <package-manager> / --no-install behave as in sv create.

Every add-on is a set of file edits, and the useful way to know one is to know which files it touches and where in this course those files are read. This is what each of the fourteen add-ons in sv add --help writes into a fresh --template minimal project, recorded by running each one alone:

  • experimental (features:async,remoteFunctions) — two flags in vite.config.ts: compilerOptions.experimental.async and experimental.remoteFunctions. Ch. 04, and the remote functions from ch. 17.
  • prettier — prettier.config.js, .prettierignore, a recommendation in .vscode/extensions.json, and scripts in package.json. Below.
  • eslint — eslint.config.js, its own editor recommendation, and scripts in package.json. Below.
  • vitest (usages:unit,component) — the test block with a browser project and a Node project in vite.config.ts, and example specs. Ch. 44.
  • playwright (demo:no) — playwright.config.ts and one spec. Ch. 46.
  • sveltekit-adapter (adapter:node) — adapter: adapter() inside sveltekit(). Ch. 48.
  • drizzle (database:sqlite+client:libsql) — drizzle.config.ts, src/lib/server/db/index.ts and schema.ts, src/env.ts, .env and .env.example. Ch. 14 and ch. 15.
  • better-auth (demo:none, and it needs drizzle) — src/lib/server/auth.ts, src/lib/server/db/auth.schema.ts, a handle in src/hooks.server.ts, and its variables in src/env.ts. Ch. 16.
  • mdsvex — preprocess and extensions inside sveltekit(). Ch. 36.
  • paraglide (languageTags:en,de,pt-br+demo:no) — project.inlang/settings.json, messages/*.json, the Vite plugin, reroute in src/hooks.ts, a handle in src/hooks.server.ts, and lang in app.html. Ch. 21.
  • enhanced-img — enhancedImages() in the plugin list, before sveltekit(). Ch. 23.
  • ai-tools — with delivery:tools, AGENTS.md, .claude/CLAUDE.md, .mcp.json and .claude/agents/svelte-file-editor.md; with delivery:plugin, .claude/settings.json. The last section of this chapter.
  • storybook — not added: .storybook/, a src/stories folder of examples and its own scripts. Ch. 40 says why two components do not need a second build system.
  • tailwindcss — not added: a Vite plugin, src/routes/layout.css and editor settings. Every colour, space and radius here is a token in tokens.css (ch. 23), and the styled component kits built on Tailwind were declined in ch. 40 for the same reason.

One thing the list does not show: an add-on writes the version ranges it was released with. On the day this was checked, the vitest add-on wrote "vitest": "^4.1.8" into package.json, and this project runs Vitest 5. The add-on gets you a working setup; keeping it current is still your job, and ch. 40 dates every version for that reason.

Community add-ons are npm packages that follow the same contract. sv add @supacool installs the package @supacool/sv (a package named sv under a scope can be shortened to the scope), sv add file:../my-addon runs one from a folder, and authors tag them with the keyword sv-add so they can be found. Each comes with a warning the documentation prints in a box: “Svelte maintainers have not reviewed community add-ons for malicious code!” An add-on is code that rewrites your files and adds dependencies, run with your permissions, so the question to ask is the one allowBuilds asks of an install script (ch. 02): have you read it? --no-download-check exists to silence the warning in a script whose add-ons you have already reviewed, and for nothing else. Writing your own — sv create --template addon, defineAddon from sv, the sv/testing helpers, publishing with sv as a peer dependency — is how you would give the eight projects in this series one shared setup; it is a project of its own, and this course leaves it there.

How an add-on can write into sveltekit() at all

SvelteKit 3 keeps its whole configuration in the sveltekit() call in vite.config.ts (ch. 04), and an add-on has to edit that call without breaking whatever is already there. It does not use string replacement. The add-ons are built on @sveltejs/sv-utils, whose svelteConfig.edit parses the config, finds the options wherever they live, and lets the add-on “address options by name” while “the helper writes each one to the right place”: Svelte-level options (compilerOptions, preprocess, extensions) sit on the object, and everything else (adapter, files, typescript, …) is a kit option, flattened onto the same sveltekit() argument. The same package owns the pnpm detail from ch. 02: pnpm.allowBuilds asks the project’s own pnpm --version and writes the unified allowBuilds map on version 11 and later, the old onlyBuiltDependencies list before that.

Preprocessors and plugins

The integrations page of the SvelteKit documentation names three kinds of thing that plug in, and this project has an opinion on each. vitePreprocess handles <style lang="scss"> and friends (style, on by default) and TypeScript that emits code (script, off by default); this project has neither — vanilla CSS needs no preprocessor, and “TypeScript is supported natively in Svelte 5”, as long as you do not use the features that emit code, which ch. 04 makes a compiler error with erasableSyntaxOnly. svelte-preprocess adds Pug, Babel and global styles; nothing here needs them. Vite plugins are the third kind, and this project has five, read in order in ch. 04: enhancedImages(), sveltekit() itself, Paraglide, the Phosphor optimiser and the project’s own bundleStats(). mdsvex is not among them: it is a preprocessor, passed to sveltekit() as preprocess.

sv check, which is svelte-check

sv check runs svelte-check, and its help says so in one line: “All svelte-check [options] are available in sv check [options]”. It type-checks the TypeScript in .svelte files, .svelte.ts modules and plain .ts alike, and it reports the Svelte compiler’s warnings — unused CSS, accessibility hints, deprecated syntax — which tsc cannot see. The project calls it directly, as svelte-check, because it is a devDependency and the scripts are the documentation:

The flags svelte-check 4.7.7 accepts, apart from --color, --no-color, --version and --help, and what this project does with each:

  • --tsconfig <path> — check exactly the files the tsconfig’s include and exclude select, TypeScript and JavaScript errors included. Used: ./tsconfig.json, whose explicit lists keep the checker out of build/ and packages/ (ch. 04) — and out of src/service-worker, which has a tsconfig of its own. That one is checked by the line’s last command, tsc -p src/service-worker, rather than by a second svelte-check --tsconfig: a folder with no .svelte file in it makes svelte-check warn that it was given nothing to do, and here a warning fails the check. Plain TypeScript is tsc’s job (ch. 39).
  • --fail-on-warnings — “Will also exit with error code when there are warnings.” Used on both scripts; the why block below says why.
  • --compiler-warnings "code:behaviour,…" — per compiler warning code, ignore or error: "css_unused_selector:ignore,a11y_missing_attribute:error" in the documentation’s example. Not used. A warning that is wrong for one line is answered on that line or fixed; silencing a code project-wide hides the same mistake everywhere else. The project once carried one of these for its custom element, and ch. 38 says why it no longer needs it.
  • --diagnostic-sources "js,svelte,css" — which of the three checkers run; all three by default. Not used.
  • --threshold warning|error — error prints only errors. Not used: every warning fails the check here, so every warning should be on the screen.
  • --output human|human-verbose|machine|machine-verbose — how to print. machine is one record per line, a timestamp and a type — START with the workspace, an ERROR or WARNING with the file, line:column and the message, COMPLETED with the totals, FAILURE if the checker itself crashed — and machine-verbose makes each diagnostic a line of JSON with its start, end, code and source. That is the format a CI step would turn into annotations on a pull request.
  • --watch and --preserveWatchOutput — keep running and re-check on every change; do not clear the screen between runs. check:watch uses the first.
  • --incremental, --tsgo and --tsgo-experimental-api — the three newest: cache the Svelte-to-TypeScript translation on disk between runs (in .svelte-kit), or hand the TypeScript diagnostics to tsgo, the Go port of the compiler that is to become TypeScript 7 (the third does the same through an API the help calls experimental, and cannot be combined with the other two). Not used: a full check of this project takes about thirteen seconds, and AGENTS.md says why this toolchain stays on TypeScript 6 for now.
  • --config <path> — the Vite config to read, for a project whose config file has another name or place. Not needed: vite.config.ts at the root is where it looks.
  • --workspace, --ignore and --no-tsconfig — declined. --no-tsconfig checks only .svelte files and skips every .ts file, and --ignore only works together with it; the tsconfig is the better list of what to check, and it is the same list the editor uses.

Why a warning fails the check

Because a warning that does not fail anything is a warning nobody reads. The project has no svelte-ignore comments at all, so every warning the compiler gives is either a mistake or a sign the compiler knows something the author did not, and both are worth stopping for. On check:watch the flag changes nothing you can see — a watching process never exits — and it is there so the two svelte-check runs differ by --watch and nothing else. The one warning a person is most likely to meet by surprise is bidirectional_control_characters, and ch. 02 says why that one in particular should stop a build.

Lint and format

Lines 1 to 35 are what sv add eslint prettier writes, unchanged; the last block is this project’s. Read top to bottom. includeIgnoreFile makes .gitignore the list of what not to lint, so a generated folder is ignored the day it is ignored by git. Then three recommended sets — JavaScript, TypeScript, Svelte — and two that switch rules *off*: eslint-config-prettier turns off every stylistic rule that would fight the formatter, and svelte.configs.prettier does the same for the Svelte plugin’s. no-undef is off on typescript-eslint’s own advice, because the TypeScript compiler already knows which globals exist and the lint rule does not. The block for **/*.svelte and **/*.svelte.ts is the important one: projectService: true gives the parser the project’s real type information, through the same TypeScript language service an editor uses, so type-aware rules work inside <script lang="ts"> and in rune modules. extraFileExtensions tells it .svelte is a source file, and parser: ts.parser is the parser for the script inside it.

The last block is a decision. svelte/prefer-svelte-reactivity asks for SvelteMap and SvelteSet wherever it sees new Map() and new Set(), which is right in a component and noise in a test that builds a fixture. Ch. 43 draws the line for application code.

This one is exactly what the prettier add-on writes: tabs, single quotes, no trailing commas, a hundred columns, and the Svelte plugin. The values matter less than having them in a file: nobody argues about formatting in a review when a command decides it.

The add-on writes a short list of lockfiles and static folders; this one is longer because it doubles as the map of everything in the project that a tool writes — the build, SvelteKit’s generated types, the end-to-end reports, the compiled messages, the library’s output, and the files the inlang SDK drops beside its settings. If a folder is in this list, do not edit it by hand: whatever writes it will write it again. pnpm run lint runs prettier --check, then ESLint, then the contrast check from ch. 23; pnpm run format rewrites everything Prettier would complain about.

The agent beside you

A language model trained on the public web has read far more Svelte 4 than Svelte 5, and far more SvelteKit 1 than 3. Asked for a component, it reaches for Svelte 4’s export let and on:click, a store where a rune belongs, an effect where a derived belongs. The Svelte team’s answer is four tools, “designed to work together, but each can be used individually”: instructions that are always in the agent’s context, an MCP server with the documentation and a static analyser, skills that load on demand, and a subagent that does Svelte work in a context window of its own. This project has all four: the instructions and the MCP configuration as committed files, the skills and the subagent through the plugin.

The instructions are the documentation’s recommended prompt, word for word: which tools exist and when to call them. They live in AGENTS.md, the file most agents read, and Claude Code reads them through a one-line import:

The MCP server comes in two forms. This file names the remote one, https://mcp.svelte.dev/mcp, which needs nothing installed and of which the documentation says “The Svelte team does not log, store, or inspect code sent to the remote server.” The local one is the @sveltejs/mcp package, started as npx -y @sveltejs/mcp, which runs the version your lockfile records — its autofixer works offline, while list-sections and get-documentation still fetch the documentation index from svelte.dev when they run; each client’s setup is a page of the AI documentation. Its four tools are the four in AGENTS.md: list-sections and get-documentation for the documentation, svelte-autofixer for static analysis, and playground-link for an ephemeral playground URL. It also offers a resource, doc-section — any documentation page attached to a conversation by the person, as svelte://<slug>.md — and a prompt, svelte-task, which a person picks to tell the model how to use the rest.

This file is the Claude Code plugin, committed. The ai-tools documentation describes what it does: “the first time you open the project you’ll be asked to trust the workspace, then it installs automatically (no /plugin install needed)”. The plugin brings the local MCP server, the skills and the subagent, and keeps them up to date. Without the committed file, the same plugin is two commands inside Claude Code: /plugin marketplace add sveltejs/ai-tools, then /plugin install svelte. The documentation lists the plugin for Claude Code and OpenCode (@sveltejs/opencode); every other client gets the individual tools. The ai-tools add-on takes four options: ide (claude-code, cursor, gemini, opencode, vscode or other), delivery (plugin or tools), tools (which individual tools, when not using the plugin) and mcpSetup (local or remote).

The subagent, svelte-file-editor, comes with the plugin rather than as a file in the project — the duplicate sv warns about above. One thing remains doubled, and it is worth knowing: in Claude Code the plugin’s local MCP server and the remote one named in .mcp.json both appear. They answer the same questions; the remote entry is kept for the clients the plugin does not cover. Its body tells it to fetch documentation, edit, run the autofixer and repeat until nothing is left. The point of a subagent is the separate context window: the documentation it reads and the autofixer rounds it goes through stay in its own conversation, and the main agent gets back the finished file and a summary.

The skills load when a task needs them. svelte-code-writer teaches the agent the @sveltejs/mcp command line; svelte-core-bestpractices is a page of Svelte 5 guidance. Most of what it says, this course builds:

  • “To compute something from state, use $derived rather than $effect” — TripState, a class whose every field is derived from one value (ch. 26).
  • “If you need to sync state to an external library such as D3, it is often neater to use {@attach ...}” — Tiptap mounted by an attachment (ch. 32).
  • “If you need to observe something external to Svelte, use createSubscriber” — the geolocation watch on the map (ch. 29, and ch. 43 for when a utility library is worth it).
  • “use $state.raw instead” for values that are replaced rather than mutated — the Tiptap editor instance in the notes tab, set when the editor mounts and cleared when it goes, never changed through Svelte (ch. 32).
  • “Prefer to use keyed each blocks … Do not use the index as a key” — keys that name the thing, on the globe and the trips list (ch. 30, 35).
  • “use clsx-style arrays and objects in class attributes, instead of the class: directive” — every conditional class (ch. 25).
  • svelte-code-writer: “Always validate - Run svelte-autofixer before finalizing any Svelte component” — the next section, which does it for every component on every build.

The autofixer, over every component

The same package has a command line. Run with a subcommand, svelte-mcp (the binary @sveltejs/mcp installs) prints its answer instead of starting a server: list-sections, get-documentation <sections>, and svelte-autofixer <code_or_path> with --svelte-version 4|5 and --async, “Wether the project is using async svelte or not”, in the help’s own spelling. This project compiles with experimental.async, so the flag belongs on every run.

An agent runs that on what it writes. The project runs it on everything it has, as a step of verify, with one rule: every issue is fixed, and every suggestion is either followed or answered in writing.

Two sources, because the app compiles with experimental.async and the library does not. The list of answered suggestions is data, so it is parsed with a valibot schema like every other input in this project: strictObject rejects a misspelt key, so an entry cannot quietly stop matching because somebody typed reasons.

The script imports svelteAutofixer — the function the svelte-autofixer command calls — instead of spawning the command fifty-five times. The command prints its result with console.log, which is Node’s inspect format and not JSON, so parsing it would mean parsing a debugging format; the package exports the function itself, with its types. All the files are analysed at once and the whole run takes a few seconds. One import comes before it, ./offline-docs.ts, for a reason that is easy to miss: importing the package also starts its MCP server, which fetches the docs index from svelte.dev and never handles a refusal. From a network svelte.dev turns away, that unhandled rejection exits the process with code 1 after a clean report. The small module answers that one request locally, because a lint step must not depend on a website.

An entry names a file, a piece of the suggestion’s text, how many times that file earns it, and the reason — which points at the comment in the code that already made the argument where one exists, so the list and the code cannot tell two stories, and otherwise states the reason itself. The count is exact in both directions. One more than accepted is a new effect nobody has looked at, and the script asks for it to be read; one fewer means the code improved and the entry outlived it, and the script asks for the entry to shrink. A list of exceptions that only ever grows stops meaning anything.

Why most of the eighty suggestions are declined, and why that is fine

Sixty-nine of them are one sentence: “You are calling a function inside an $effect. Please check if the function is reassigning a stateful variable … Ignore this suggestion if you are sure this function is not assigning any stateful variable.” It is a question, not a verdict, because the analyser cannot see inside the function. In this project the functions are MapLibre’s, three.js’s, Tiptap’s, timers and layout measurements — exactly what effects are for — and the entries say so file by file. The other eleven are three effects that assign state on purpose (a timer, a measurement, a colour only a styled page can answer) and eight bind:this that an attachment cannot replace because the element is used from more than one place. What the gate guarantees is not zero suggestions; it is that the next one gets read.

Checkpoint

  • You can write the sv create line for a new project with the add-ons you need, without answering a prompt.
  • You can say which files each of the add-ons this project uses wrote, and where in the course each file is read.
  • You know what --fail-on-warnings, --compiler-warnings and --output machine-verbose do, and why this project uses only the first.
  • You can say what the four Svelte AI tools are, which files configure them here, and what pnpm run lint:svelte adds to verify.
